name: Aaron Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the Valley Power depot on Station Road at half six, and the first thing is the tailboard talk, where the foreman, Dale, goes over the day's jobs and the hazards. Most days I'm ground crew: I rig the ropes, send tools and cross-arms up to the lads in the bucket truck, and keep the site tidy so nobody trips. I'm a second-year apprentice at 58, which makes me the oldest beginner they've ever had. I did 31 years rigging at the shipyard in Harlow before it shut, so the ropes are easy, but climbing poles still scares me a bit.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside with a crew again, and I like that when we leave, somebody's lights are on. What wears me out is the learning. I failed my pole-top rescue test the first time, and my knees told me about it for a week. And the paperwork's all on a tablet now, which I can't stand, so Sam, the 23-year-old apprentice I eat lunch with, reads the work orders out to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the canteen for two years: told you so. It's the same as every other gadget the bosses got excited about. You still need somebody to climb up and splice the wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish what I started. I need seven more years to build a decent pension at Valley Power, because the shipyard one is small. If nothing big changes, I just keep my head down and get my ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep going, pass my climbing assessment in the spring, and finish the apprenticeship by the end of next year. I wouldn't change a thing at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relief, mostly. Like when the forecast says rain and it turns out fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet. Even in this picture, where AI only does small things, would any of it reach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office uses it to plan our routes, or to sort out which poles get inspected first. That's fine by me as long as it's Dale who decides if a pole is safe to climb. A computer has never had to stand under a rotten pole in the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And at home, would anything change for you and your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Mags keeps cooking at the primary school, we pay the mortgage, and we see the grandkids on Sundays. We've got about four months put by from my shipyard payout, and in this picture that just sits there, which is how I like it.

S0.say: He'd tell the canteen he was right all along: AI is another gadget the bosses got excited about, and someone still has to climb up and splice the wire.
S0.think: Privately he sees this as the picture where he finishes what he started. He needs about seven more years at Valley Power to build a pension, because his shipyard pension is small.
S0.do: Carries on as normal: passes his climbing assessment in the spring and finishes the apprenticeship by the end of next year. Leaves the four months of savings untouched and changes nothing at home.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a forecast of rain that turns out fine.
S0.quote: A computer has never had to stand under a rotten pole in the wind.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron came into line work at 56 after the shipyard closed, and everything he says is framed by the pension he still needs to build. He's comfortable with AI planning routes as long as a person decides on safety. His dislike of the tablet is already a sign of how much he leans on younger workmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union branch meeting I'd stand up and say: no new tech on our crews without an agreement. Training on company time, nobody laid off because of it, and the union in the room when they decide. That's what we didn't get at the shipyard, and look how that ended.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the slowest learner on the crew and everybody knows it. If they bring in drones for inspections and smart tablets for everything, it's me who gets left behind, not Sam. They still need hands on the poles, but they need fewer of them if the planning gets clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the branch secretary, Lorraine, this winter and get this on the agenda before the company moves. I'd keep going with my apprenticeship and not miss a single training day. And I'd swallow my pride and get Sam to show me the tablet properly, just the bits I need, not the fancy stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a creak in the hull and not knowing yet if it's anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatchers and the meter readers, more than us. Brenda in dispatch has been taking storm calls for twenty years, and that's exactly the sort of job a clever computer takes. I'd want the union fighting for her as hard as for the linemen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI, but you'd learn the tablet. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The tablet's a tool I can hold, like a meter or a rope. The AI stuff is something else, something that thinks for you, and I don't want it thinking for me. I'll learn the minimum to keep my job and not one button more.

S1.say: He'd stand up at the union branch meeting and demand an agreement before any new tech reaches the crews. He wants training on company time, no layoffs, and the union in the room.
S1.think: Privately he knows he's the slowest learner on the crew and the most likely to be left behind by drones and smart tablets. He thinks clever planning means fewer hands on poles, even if hands are still needed.
S1.do: Asks the branch secretary to put new technology on the agenda this winter, before the company acts. Keeps going with the apprenticeship without missing a training day and gets a young workmate to teach him the basics of the tablet.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a creak in the hull before knowing whether it matters.
S1.quote: I'll learn the minimum to keep my job and not one button more.
S1.fieldNote: His first move is always collective: get it on the union agenda before the company acts, which comes straight from losing the shipyard. Behind that he's frank that he is the weak link on his crew. He draws a firm line between tools he can hold and AI that thinks for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say there must be a law: no robot works a live line without a human crew, and if a company replaces workers with machines, those workers get a share of what it saves. I'd be at the rally, and I'd make Mags's nephew put it on the internet for me, because I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I've seen this film. When the yard closed, the young ones got retrained and the old ones got a handshake. I'm old and junior at the same time, which is the worst of both. In two years I'd be 60, with four years in the Valley Power pension. That's nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough to do much except brace. I'd stop the holiday we were saving for, sell Mags's old hatchback, and put every spare bit into savings to stretch four months to maybe eight. I'd push the union for proper redundancy terms and ask the pension people, in writing, what I'd get if I went at 60.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, if I'm honest. It's the same feeling as the morning they put the notice up at the yard gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mags that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, love, here we go again. She'd say we've done it once and we can do it again, because that's her. But she was 52 last time, and now she's on her feet in a hot kitchen all day, and I don't want her carrying us both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money got tight, which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, if I can help it. I'd cut everything else first: the car, the darts league, the takeaway on Fridays. The mortgage has about three years left and I'd sooner eat beans than miss one payment of it.

S2.say: He'd demand a law that no robot works a live line without a human crew, and that replaced workers get a share of the savings. He'd go to the rally and have a relative post his views online.
S2.think: Privately he expects to be treated like the older men at the shipyard: a handshake, not a retraining. At 60 with only four years in the Valley Power pension, he thinks being both old and junior is the worst position to be in.
S2.do: Cancels the planned holiday, sells his partner's old hatchback and puts every spare amount into savings, aiming to stretch four months to about eight. Pushes the union for redundancy terms and asks the pension fund in writing what he'd get at 60.
S2.feel: Sick, like the morning the closure notice went up at the shipyard gate.
S2.quote: I'm old and junior at the same time, which is the worst of both.
S2.fieldNote: Two years of warning gives Aaron nothing but time to brace, and he says so plainly. His public anger and his private fear point the same way, because he has already lived through a closure. The mortgage is the line he won't cross; everything else gets cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse. The government and the company have to sit down with the union now, not when the robots turn up. I'd say that at every meeting till they're sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years changes my sums. I'd be 63, the mortgage would be paid off in March 2030, and I'd have my full ticket as a qualified line worker. It still hurts, but it's a soft landing instead of a crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, no question, because a qualified man is harder to let go. I'd put the money from the mortgage into savings once it's paid off. And through the union I'd push for a bridge, some payment to carry older workers from when the job goes to when the pension starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not sick. More like a long drive with the fuel light on, where you think you'll make the station.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly do those extra three years buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three more years of pension, the house paid off, and a chance to go out on my own feet instead of being pushed. At the yard I was carried out on a list. If I have to go, I want to choose the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, actually. He's 23 and he's betting his whole life on this trade. I'd tell him to keep his ticket but learn whatever runs these robots, because I think the young ones will need two trades, and I don't think I could manage one more.

S3.say: He'd tell every meeting that five years leaves no excuse: government and the company must sit down with the union now, before the robots arrive.
S3.think: Privately he sees five years as the difference between a crash and a soft landing. He'd be 63, with the mortgage paid off in March 2030 and his full qualification as a line worker.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship so he's harder to let go, and moves the former mortgage payment into savings from 2030. Pushes through the union for a bridge payment that carries older workers until their pension starts.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like driving with the fuel light on and expecting to make the station.
S3.quote: At the yard I was carried out on a list. If I have to go, I want to choose the day.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter to Aaron mostly in money terms: pension years, the mortgage gone, a qualification in hand. What he wants most is dignity, choosing his own leaving day. His worry quickly shifts to the young apprentice, which says a lot about his union instincts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get it right, so if they get it wrong it's a choice, not an accident. I'd want it written into law now: what happens to workers, who gets the money the machines make. I'd be saying that at the union and at the ballot box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selfishly, I'm all right. I'd retire at 65 in 2033 and be watching it from my garden. But my grandson Leo would be 17 in 2036, just when he'd be looking for an apprenticeship like mine, and that keeps me up more than my own job does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, finish my ticket, work to 65 like I planned, and take my pension. Meanwhile I'd stay active in the branch and vote for whoever promises to share the gains with working people. I'd tell my son Tom, who drives a forklift, to start looking at what's next now, while he's 31.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about me, a bit uneasy about the family. It's like seeing a storm out at sea that will land after you've gone home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be retired before it lands. So why keep campaigning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody fought for the little shipyard pension I've got, and I never met them. You pay it forward. My dad used to say the union is a rope: it only works if everyone keeps hold of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him not to wait for a notice on a gate like I did. Do a course in the evenings, something with your hands that also needs a head, maybe repairing these machines. And join the union wherever he ends up.

S4.say: He'd argue that ten years leaves no excuse, so getting it wrong would be a choice. He'd want laws now on what happens to workers and who gets the money machines make, and he'd say it at the union and the ballot box.
S4.think: Privately he knows he'd retire at 65 in 2033 and be largely safe. What worries him is his grandson, who'd be 17 and looking for an apprenticeship just as AGI arrives.
S4.do: Carries on, finishes his qualification and retires at 65 as planned. Stays active in the union branch, votes for politicians who promise to share the gains, and urges his 31-year-old son to start evening courses now.
S4.feel: Calm about himself and uneasy about his family, like a storm at sea that will land after he's gone home.
S4.quote: My dad used to say the union is a rope: it only works if everyone keeps hold of it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning, Aaron's own risk almost disappears and his worry moves to his son and grandson. He keeps campaigning out of loyalty rather than self-interest, which fits his whole story. His advice to his son is the advice he wishes he'd had before the shipyard closed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. I'd be 60, junior, with almost nothing in the pension, and I'd be one of thousands of older men looking for something. What would help is a bridge to the pension at 60 without a penalty, agreed by the union and paid by the companies that save money on the robots. Don't offer me a computer course. Offer me a fair way out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the shipyard, and that's the whole story for me. I've been made redundant once by men in suits who never touched a rope. I'm not doing it twice quietly. Put that in your report.

headlineQuote: I've been made redundant once by men in suits who never touched a rope. I'm not doing it twice quietly.
portrait: Aaron Tanaka is a 58-year-old second-year apprentice at Valley Power, a publicly owned electricity company, who came into line work after 31 years as a rigger at a shipyard that closed. He's a lifelong union man who avoids new technology, gets a young workmate to read the tablet for him and never uses AI. In the mild pictures he just wants to finish his ticket and build the pension he still needs. AGI in two years alarms him because he'd be 60, junior and short of pension years, and he would cut spending, save hard and fight through the union. With five or ten years he calms down, plans to retire on his own terms, and turns his worry to his son and grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries him most, because he'd be 60, junior and almost without a Valley Power pension, competing with thousands of older workers.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge to his pension at 60 without a penalty, agreed by the union and paid for by companies that save money on robots, rather than a computer course.
